definition: To discourage someone from doing something, usually by making it seem risky, costly or unpleasant.
example: Steep ticket prices may deter some families from visiting the science museum.
nuance: Deter usually works through fear, cost or obstacles, while dissuade usually means talking someone out of an action.
prompt: A town wants fewer people to leave trash at a scenic overlook.
options: A sign announcing a hefty fine should deter visitors from dumping trash there.
The town hoped free picnic tables would deter more families to come and enjoy the view.
The council voted to deter the cleanup meeting until next spring.
Volunteers deter the litter each Saturday by hauling it to the recycling center.
reasons: The threat of a penalty makes littering seem costly, so people choose not to do it.
This reverses the meaning: the word turns people away from an action and never draws them toward one.
Putting off a meeting is "defer," a look-alike that means to postpone.
Removing trash after it is dropped cleans up the mess but discourages no one from dropping it.

practice.prompt: A student is thinking about signing up for a demanding advanced chemistry class.
options: After reading the syllabus, she could deter which units would be hardest for her.
She refused to let the heavy workload deter her from enrolling in the course.
The teacher's warm welcome helped deter her into joining the class right away.
She asked the counselor to deter her enrollment until the fall semester.
reasons: The word is not short for "determine"; it means to discourage, not to figure something out.
The workload could have scared her off, but she didn't let it stop her.
A friendly welcome pulls someone toward a choice, which is the opposite of what this verb does.
Delaying something to a later date is "defer," not this word.
